questions.title: Endoneurium's connective tissue type
questions.question: Endoneurium is a:-

options.A: CT covering of the nerve trunk
options.B: Dense CT that surrounds the bundles of nerve fibers
options.C: Dense CT that surrounds single nerve fiber
options.D: Loose CT that divides the nerve trunk into bundles
options.E: Loose CT that separates the individual nerve fibers

explanations.A: Incorrect. Covering the whole nerve trunk from the outside is the epineurium's job, the outermost of the nerve's three connective tissue layers, not the endoneurium, which sits at the innermost, single-fibre level.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A dense connective tissue layer around a bundle of fibres describes the perineurium, the fascicle-level covering. The endoneurium is loose, not dense, and wraps one fibre, not a bundle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The endoneurium is correctly placed at the single-fibre level, but it is loose connective tissue, not dense — density is what marks the perineurium instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. No connective tissue layer divides the trunk into bundles by that description; the perineurium groups fibres into fascicles rather than dividing a pre-formed bundle.
explanations.E: Correct. The endoneurium is the innermost of the nerve's three connective tissue coverings — a thin sleeve of loose connective tissue, carrying reticular fibres and capillaries, that surrounds each individual nerve fibre and its Schwann cell sheath. It sits inside the denser perineurium, which bundles many endoneurium-wrapped fibres into a fascicle, and the epineurium, which binds the fascicles into the whole nerve trunk. Being loose and fibre-level, rather than dense and fascicle- or trunk-level, is exactly what identifies it here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the endoneurium as the loose connective tissue sleeve around a single nerve fibre.
questions.module_subject: MANS-HBG > Histology > Nervous Tissue > Peripheral nerve coverings

questions.title: The phase with chromosomes at the equator
questions.question: The phase in which chromosomes become arranged in the center or equator of the cell is:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Anaphase is the stage after this one, when the sister chromatids, already aligned at the equator, separate and move toward opposite poles.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Interphase is not a division stage at all — it is the period between divisions (G1, S, G2) when the cell grows and replicates its DNA, well before any chromosome alignment.
explanations.C: Correct. Metaphase is the stage of mitosis at which the condensed chromosomes, each still made of two sister chromatids, become arranged at the equatorial (metaphase) plate, the imaginary plane midway between the two spindle poles, attached to spindle microtubules via their kinetochores. This alignment is a checkpoint: the cell verifies every chromosome is correctly attached before anaphase is allowed to begin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Prophase is the stage before this one, when chromosomes condense and become visible but have not yet aligned at the cell's equator.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Telophase is the final stage, when the chromosomes have already reached the poles and the nuclear envelope reforms around each daughter set.

questions.learning_objective: Name metaphase as the mitotic stage at which chromosomes align at the cell's equator.

questions.title: Cri-du-chat syndrome's deleted chromosome
questions.question: Cri-du-chat syndrome is caused due to partial deletion of one arm of:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. The 4th chromosome is not the one deleted in Cri-du-chat syndrome; a different short-arm deletion, of the 4th chromosome, produces the unrelated Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome instead.
explanations.B: Correct. Cri-du-chat syndrome is a structural chromosomal abnormality caused by partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-). The name, French for cat's cry, refers to the high-pitched, cat-like cry of affected infants, alongside microcephaly, characteristic facial features and intellectual disability.
explanations.C: Incorrect. No standard named syndrome in this exam's scope is attributed to a 6th chromosome deletion; Cri-du-chat is specifically a 5th chromosome (5p) deletion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The 7th chromosome is not the site of the Cri-du-chat deletion.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The 8th chromosome is not the site of the Cri-du-chat deletion.

questions.learning_objective: Name chromosome 5's short arm as the site of the Cri-du-chat deletion.

questions.title: Klinefelter syndrome's karyotype
questions.question: What is the karyotyping of Klinefelter's syndrome:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. 47,XYY describes Jacob's syndrome (an extra Y chromosome in a male), a different, generally milder karyotype from Klinefelter's.
explanations.B: Correct. Klinefelter's syndrome is 47,XXY: a male karyotype with an extra X chromosome, arising from non-disjunction during meiosis in either parent. Affected males typically show tall stature, small testes, infertility and gynaecomastia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 45,XO is Turner's syndrome, a female with only one sex chromosome, not Klinefelter's.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 47,XXX is Triple X syndrome, a female karyotype, not Klinefelter's, which is a male (XY-based) condition.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 48,XXXX is a rarer female sex-chromosome polysomy, not the male Klinefelter karyotype.

questions.learning_objective: State the Klinefelter syndrome karyotype as 47,XXY.

questions.title: The structure formed at the end of prophase
questions.question: Which of the following structures is formed at the end of prophase:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chromosomal condensation is a process that happens during prophase, not a discrete structure formed at its end.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Separation of sister chromatids is an event of anaphase, well after prophase has ended.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cleavage furrow appears during cytokinesis, at the very end of the division, not at the end of prophase.
explanations.D: Correct. By the end of prophase each condensed chromosome's centromere has assembled its kinetochore, the protein plate on which the spindle's microtubules will attach. This attachment is what lets the two sister chromatids be pulled apart to opposite poles once anaphase begins. The kinetochore therefore has to be in place before metaphase alignment or anaphase separation can happen at all.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The nucleolus disappears, rather than forms, toward the end of prophase, as the nucleus prepares to break down.

questions.learning_objective: State that the kinetochore, the spindle-attachment structure, is assembled by the end of prophase.

questions.title: Where the eccrine sweat gland duct opens
questions.question: Duct of Eccrine sweat gland opens in the:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. The eccrine duct traverses the dermis and epidermis on its way out; it does not terminate or open within the deep dermis itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Opening into the hair follicle is the apocrine sweat gland's route, not the eccrine gland's — this is exactly the distinction that separates the two duct-opening sites.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The hair papilla is a dermal structure at the base of the hair bulb, unrelated to where a sweat gland duct discharges.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The nail bed is not a site any sweat gland duct opens into.
explanations.E: Correct. The eccrine (merocrine) sweat gland's straight excretory duct pierces the epidermis independently of any hair follicle and opens directly onto the free surface of the skin. This is unlike the apocrine sweat gland, whose duct instead opens into the upper part of a hair follicle. The duct's opening site is the landmark that separates the two gland types once their secretory mechanism has already been asked about.

questions.learning_objective: State that the eccrine sweat gland duct opens directly onto the skin surface.

questions.title: A chromosomal deletion syndrome
questions.question: Which syndrome is an example of chromosomal deletion:-

explanations.A: Correct. Cri-du-chat syndrome results from partial loss of the short arm of chromosome 5. That loss of a piece of a chromosome, rather than a whole extra or missing chromosome, is what makes it structural rather than numerical. It is the standard example examiners use of a structural chromosomal deletion, set against the numerical abnormalities offered as the other options.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Down syndrome is a numerical abnormality, trisomy 21, an extra whole chromosome 21, not a structural deletion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Galactosemia is an inborn error of metabolism from a single-gene enzyme deficiency, not a chromosomal deletion syndrome at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Klinefelter's syndrome (47,XXY) is a numerical sex-chromosome abnormality, an extra whole X chromosome, not a structural deletion.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Turner's syndrome (45,XO) is a numerical abnormality, a missing whole sex chromosome, not a structural deletion.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Cri-du-chat as the example of a structural (deletion) chromosomal abnormality among numerical-abnormality syndromes.

questions.title: The organelle synthesising secretory protein
questions.question: Which of the followings is responsible for synthesis of secretory proteins:-

explanations.A: Correct. Attached (rough-ER-bound) ribosomes make the proteins destined to leave the cell. As each chain grows, it is threaded directly into the rough endoplasmic reticulum's lumen rather than released into the cytosol. This is what marks a protein for the secretory pathway, on to the Golgi apparatus and then export, rather than for the cell's own cytoplasmic use.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Free ribosomes, suspended in the cytosol, synthesise proteins the cell keeps for its own cytoplasmic use, not proteins destined for secretion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lysosomes digest material; they do not synthesise protein.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peroxisomes are oxidative organelles handling detoxification and fatty acid breakdown; they play no role in protein synthesis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes altogether and instead handles lipid synthesis, calcium storage and detoxification, not protein synthesis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify attached (rough-ER) ribosomes as the site of secretory protein synthesis.

questions.title: The structure that transports organelles inside the cell
questions.question: Which of the followings is related to transport of organelles inside cell:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus packages and modifies proteins for export; it is a destination and processing station for transported cargo, not the transport track itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Intermediate filaments provide mechanical, structural support to the cell rather than serving as tracks for organelle movement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lipid droplets are storage inclusions, not a transport structure.
explanations.D: Correct. Microtubules form the tracks along which motor proteins carry vesicles and organelles from one part of the cell to another. Kinesin walks toward the microtubule's plus end and dynein toward its minus end, giving transport a direction as well as a track. The same microtubule system also positions the mitotic spindle during cell division.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Ribosomes translate mRNA into protein; they play no role in intracellular transport of organelles.

questions.learning_objective: Identify microtubules as the cytoskeletal element that tracks organelle transport inside the cell.

questions.title: The function that makes the nucleolus prominent
questions.question: Nucleolus is prominent in cells active in which of the following functions:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lipid metabolism is carried out mainly by the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, not signalled by a prominent nucleolus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bile acid metabolism is a hepatocyte-specific function unrelated to nucleolar prominence.
explanations.C: Correct. The nucleolus is the site of ribosomal RNA transcription and ribosome subunit assembly. A cell that is especially active in protein synthesis needs a correspondingly high output of ribosomes to build that protein. That demand is what makes its nucleolus large and prominent.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Immune function does not, by itself, predict nucleolar prominence; it is protein-synthetic activity specifically that does.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Phagocytic function relies on lysosomal digestion, not on a prominent nucleolus.

questions.learning_objective: Relate nucleolar prominence to high protein-synthetic activity via ribosome production.

questions.title: The epithelium type of the epidermis
questions.question: What is the type of epithelium found in the epidermis of skin:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pseudostratified columnar epithelium lines the respiratory tract, not the epidermis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Simple squamous epithelium is a single flat cell layer, far too thin to be the many-layered, protective epidermis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Stratified columnar epithelium is a rare epithelium type found at a few transitional sites (parts of the conjunctiva, large excretory ducts); it does not describe the epidermis.
explanations.D: Correct. The epidermis is stratified squamous keratinized epithelium. It is many layers thick, its cells flattening as they rise toward the surface. The outermost layer is capped by a dead, keratin-filled horny layer that gives the skin its protective, waterproof barrier.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium lines wet internal surfaces such as the oesophagus and vagina; the epidermis is specifically keratinized, which is what makes it suited to the dry external surface.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the epidermis as stratified squamous keratinized epithelium.

questions.title: The true statement about the neuron's axon
questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding the axon of nerve cell:-

options.B: Carry impulse away from the cell body
options.C: Carry impulse to the cell body
options.E: Single & then divide into T-shaped branches in bipolar cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. A multipolar neuron has many dendrites but, like every neuron, at most one axon — the axon is not multiplied along with the dendrites.
explanations.B: Correct. The axon is the neuron's single process that conducts the nerve impulse away from the cell body, toward a synapse, muscle or gland. This is the opposite direction from a dendrite, which instead conducts an impulse toward the cell body. Direction of conduction, not process count or branching, is what identifies an axon in any neuron shape.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Carrying an impulse toward the cell body describes a dendrite's direction of conduction, not the axon's.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An axon is typically unbranched or only sparsely branched along most of its length, branching mainly at its terminal end; extensive branching is more characteristic of dendrites.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A T-shaped bifurcation into two branches describes the single process of a pseudounipolar (not bipolar) sensory neuron, which splits into a peripheral and a central branch.

questions.learning_objective: State that the axon conducts the nerve impulse away from the cell body.

questions.title: The syndrome also known as Trisomy 21
questions.question: Which syndrome is also known as Trisomy 21:-

explanations.A: Correct. Down syndrome is trisomy 21, the presence of three copies of chromosome 21 instead of the usual two. It arises most often from maternal meiosis I non-disjunction, where the homologous chromosome pair fails to separate. The extra chromosome 21 produces the syndrome's characteristic facial features, hypotonia and intellectual disability.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Edward's syndrome is trisomy 18, an extra chromosome 18, a different and generally more severe numerical abnormality.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Klinefelter's syndrome is 47,XXY, an extra sex chromosome, not an autosomal trisomy 21.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Patau syndrome is trisomy 13, an extra chromosome 13.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Turner's syndrome is 45,XO, a missing sex chromosome, the opposite of a trisomy.

questions.learning_objective: Name Down syndrome as trisomy 21.

questions.title: The main function of intracellular digestion
questions.question: Intracellular digestion is the main function of:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus packages and modifies proteins for export or delivery; it does not digest material.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The endoplasmic reticulum synthesises protein (rough) or lipid and handles calcium storage and detoxification (smooth); digestion is not its role.
explanations.C: Correct. The lysosome is the membrane-bound organelle packed with acid hydrolase enzymes. Those enzymes carry out intracellular digestion, breaking down engulfed extracellular material or the cell's own aged organelles. What cannot be digested is left behind as a residual body.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A residual body is what remains after a lysosome's digestion is incomplete — a leftover product, not the digesting organelle itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Ribosomes translate mRNA into protein; they play no digestive role.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the lysosome as the organelle responsible for intracellular digestion.

questions.title: The epithelium describing blood vascular endothelium
questions.question: Which of the followings describe the blood vascular endothelium:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Simple cuboidal epithelium lines structures such as small ducts and renal tubules, not the vascular endothelium.
explanations.B: Correct. The endothelium lining every blood vessel, from the aorta down to a capillary, is simple squamous epithelium. It is a single layer of flattened cells resting on a basal lamina. Its thinness minimises the diffusion distance for gases and solutes crossing between blood and tissue.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Simple columnar epithelium lines absorptive/secretory surfaces such as the intestine, not blood vessels.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Stratified squamous epithelium, many cell layers thick, lines surfaces subject to abrasion (skin, oesophagus); the thin, single-layer endothelium is the opposite of this.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Pseudostratified columnar epithelium lines the respiratory tract, not blood vessels.

questions.learning_objective: Classify vascular endothelium as simple squamous epithelium.
questions.module_subject: MANS-HBG > Histology > Cardiovascular > Blood vessel wall

questions.title: The CT cell with a signet ring appearance in H&E
questions.question: Which of the following connective tissue cells have signet ring appearance with Hematoxylin and Eosin stain:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mast cells show numerous small cytoplasmic granules on H&E (though these are better demonstrated by toluidine blue's metachromasia), not a signet-ring shape.
explanations.B: Correct. The white (unilocular) adipose cell stores fat as one large lipid droplet. That droplet dissolves out during routine tissue processing, leaving a large empty-looking vacuole. It pushes the flattened nucleus out to the cell's periphery, giving the classic signet-ring appearance seen in H&E.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The brown (multilocular) adipose cell instead holds many small lipid droplets around a more central nucleus, not one large droplet with a peripheral nucleus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Reticular cells are star-shaped cells associated with reticular fibres in organ stroma; they do not show a signet-ring appearance.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Macrophages have an irregular shape with a kidney-shaped or oval nucleus and granular, vacuolated cytoplasm, not the single-large-droplet signet-ring look.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the white adipose cell's single large lipid droplet as the cause of its signet-ring H&E appearance.
questions.module_subject: MANS-HBG > Histology > Connective Tissue > Types of connective tissue proper

questions.title: The connective tissue proper prominent in newborn infants
questions.question: Which of the following types of connective tissue proper is prominent in newly born infants:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Loose connective tissue is present throughout life and is not the tissue specifically prominent in the newborn period.
explanations.B: Correct. Brown adipose tissue is multilocular and rich in mitochondria, which it uses for non-shivering thermogenesis. It is abundant in fetal life and in the newborn, when temperature regulation by shivering is still poorly developed. It is then progressively lost through childhood and largely replaced by white fat.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Elastic tissue (ligamenta flava, some large vessel walls) is not the tissue characteristic of the newborn period.
explanations.D: Incorrect. White (unilocular) adipose tissue is the fat that predominates in adults, not the newborn-prominent brown fat.
explanations.E: Incorrect. White fibrous (dense regular collagenous) tissue, found in tendons and ligaments, is not specifically prominent in newborns.

questions.learning_objective: State that brown adipose tissue is abundant in fetal life and the newborn, unlike white fat.

questions.title: The cell that synthesises myelin in the PNS
questions.question: Which of the following cells synthesize myelin in peripheral nervous system:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Microglia are the CNS's resident phagocytic, monocyte-derived cell; they do not myelinate.
explanations.B: Correct. The Schwann cell is a neural-crest-derived peripheral glial cell. It wraps its own plasma membrane repeatedly around a single segment, an internode, of one peripheral axon. The compacted, lipid-rich layers of that wrapping form the myelin sheath, one Schwann cell supplying one internode.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ependymal cells line the CNS's fluid-filled cavities (ventricles, central canal); they do not myelinate.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Astrocytes support and nourish CNS neurons and help form the blood-brain barrier; myelination is not their function.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The oligodendrocyte is the CNS's myelinating cell, not the peripheral nervous system's — that peripheral role belongs to the Schwann cell instead.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the Schwann cell as the myelin-forming cell of the peripheral nervous system.

questions.title: The stain suitable for centriole staining
questions.question: Which of the following is suitable for centriole staining:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Routine H&E does not reliably resolve the centriole, a structure too fine for this general-purpose stain to demonstrate clearly.
explanations.B: Correct. Iron hematoxylin has a strong affinity for the centriole's dense protein structure. It stains the centriole as a deeply basophilic dot, or pair of dots, near the nucleus. This is a structural stain, not one tied to a specific enzyme the way the other options are.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acid phosphatase is the histochemical stain for lysosomes, demonstrating their enzyme content, not the centriole.
explanations.D: Incorrect. PAS (periodic acid-Schiff) demonstrates carbohydrate-rich structures such as glycogen and the basement membrane, not the centriole.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Best's carmine stains glycogen, unrelated to centriole demonstration.

questions.learning_objective: Name iron hematoxylin as the stain that demonstrates the centriole.

questions.title: The site lined by simple squamous epithelium
questions.question: Simple squamous epithelium is found in which of the following sites:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Most renal tubule segments are lined by simple cuboidal epithelium, not simple squamous.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The urinary bladder is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), which changes shape with distension, not by simple squamous epithelium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The body of the uterus is lined by simple columnar epithelium (endometrium), not simple squamous.
explanations.D: Correct. The lung alveolus is lined predominantly by Type I pneumocytes, extremely thin simple squamous cells. They cover about 95% of the alveolar surface and minimise the diffusion distance for gas exchange. The remaining surface belongs to the fewer, cuboidal, surfactant-secreting Type II pneumocytes.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Thin skin's epidermis is stratified squamous keratinized epithelium, many layers thick, not a single squamous layer.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the lung alveolus as lined by simple squamous epithelium (Type I pneumocytes).

questions.title: A general character of epithelial tissue
questions.question: Which of the followings is a character of epithelial tissue:-

options.A: Cells do not rest on basement membrane
options.B: There is continuous degeneration and regeneration
options.C: Widely separated cells with little intercellular substance
options.D: There are blood vessels between cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. Epithelial cells characteristically do rest on a basement membrane, which separates them from the underlying connective tissue; the opposite of this option is the true character.
explanations.B: Correct. Epithelial surfaces face constant wear, whether from the exterior, a body cavity or a lumen. Because of that wear, epithelium has a high, continuous capacity for regeneration. Its basal or otherwise proliferative cells divide by mitosis throughout life to replace whatever is lost from the surface.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Epithelial cells are closely packed with minimal intercellular substance between them; wide separation with abundant intercellular substance instead describes connective tissue.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Epithelium is avascular — no blood vessel penetrates between epithelial cells, which are instead nourished by diffusion from the underlying connective tissue across the basement membrane.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Nerve endings, unlike blood vessels, can and do enter between epithelial cells, for example the free nerve endings supplying the epidermis.

questions.learning_objective: List continuous mitotic regeneration among the general characters of epithelial tissue.
questions.module_subject: MANS-HBG > Histology > Epithelial Tissue > General character

questions.title: The connective tissue cell rich in lysosomes
questions.question: Which of the following CT cells is rich in lysosomes:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fibroblasts are synthetic cells, rich in rough endoplasmic reticulum for collagen production, not characteristically lysosome-rich.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mast cells are packed with metachromatic secretory granules (heparin, histamine), a distinct granule population from lysosomes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Plasma cells are rich in rough endoplasmic reticulum for antibody synthesis, not lysosomes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adipose cells are dominated by their single large lipid droplet, with minimal other organelle content.
explanations.E: Correct. The macrophage is connective tissue's resident member of the mononuclear phagocyte system. That phagocytic job needs enzymes, which is why the macrophage is rich in lysosomes. The acid hydrolases they supply digest whatever the cell has phagocytosed, bacteria, debris and worn-out cells among them.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the macrophage as the connective tissue cell rich in lysosomes.

questions.title: The cell responsible for heparin secretion
questions.question: Which of the following cells is responsible for heparin secretion:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fibroblasts synthesise collagen and ground substance; heparin is not among their secreted products.
explanations.B: Correct. The mast cell's cytoplasmic granules store heparin and histamine. They are released when an allergen cross-links IgE already bound to receptors on the cell's surface. This degranulation is the basis of an immediate, type I, hypersensitivity reaction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Plasma cells secrete antibodies (immunoglobulins), not heparin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adipose cells store and release fat, not heparin.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Macrophages secrete a wide range of cytokines and enzymes as part of phagocytic and immune signalling, but heparin secretion is specifically the mast cell's role.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the mast cell as the source of heparin secretion.

questions.title: A character of dorsal root ganglia
questions.question: Which of the following is a character of dorsal root ganglia:-

options.A: Cell bodies are mostly of a small uniform size
options.C: Have incomplete capsule of satellite cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. Dorsal root ganglion (pseudounipolar sensory) cell bodies are large and fairly uniform, not small — small, uniform-size cell bodies instead describe autonomic ganglion neurons.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cell bodies in a dorsal root ganglion are grouped in clusters (often at the periphery of the ganglion), not simply scattered at random.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dorsal root ganglion neurons have a complete capsule of flattened satellite cells around each cell body, not an incomplete one.
explanations.D: Correct. The dorsal root (sensory) ganglion is relatively poorly vascularised. This helps distinguish it from an autonomic ganglion, whose blood supply is richer. That richer supply matches the autonomic ganglion's own greater metabolic activity, since its neurons synapse rather than simply relaying a fibre through.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The dorsal root ganglion's connective tissue capsule, continuous with the epineurium of the dorsal root, is a proper investing capsule, not distinctively thin.

questions.learning_objective: State that the dorsal root ganglion is relatively poorly vascularised compared with an autonomic ganglion.

questions.title: The stage of DNA synthesis and chromosome doubling
questions.question: DNA is synthesized and chromosome number is doubled in which of the following stages:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. G1 phase precedes DNA replication; the cell grows and prepares but chromosomes are still unreplicated (single chromatid, 46-s) throughout G1.
explanations.B: Correct. S phase is when the cell replicates its DNA. That replication converts each of the 46 single-chromatid chromosomes (46-s) into a double-chromatid chromosome (46-d). The chromosome count itself stays at 46 throughout; it is only the chromatid content of each chromosome that doubles.
explanations.C: Incorrect. G0 is a resting, non-cycling state some cells enter instead of proceeding through the cycle; no DNA replication happens there.
explanations.D: Incorrect. G2 phase follows S phase, after replication is already complete, and is a preparatory gap before mitosis, not the replication stage itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Meiosis is not itself a chromosome-doubling stage; the doubling by DNA replication occurs in the S phase that precedes meiosis I, exactly as it does before mitosis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify S phase as when DNA is replicated and each chromosome's chromatid content doubles.

questions.title: The routine histological stain
questions.question: Which of the following stains is used for routine histological examination:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Wright's stain is used for blood and bone marrow smears, not routine tissue histology.
explanations.B: Correct. Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) is the routine, general-purpose stain applied to essentially every tissue section. Haematoxylin, a basic dye, colours basophilic structures such as nuclei blue to purple. Eosin, an acidic dye, colours acidophilic structures such as most cytoplasm and collagen pink to red.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sudan stain demonstrates lipid specifically; it is a special stain, not the routine one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Silver impregnation is the special stain for reticular fibres, not the routine, general-purpose stain.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Masson's trichrome is the special stain used to highlight collagen distinctly from muscle; it is reserved for that purpose, not used routinely on every section.

questions.learning_objective: Name H&E as the routine histological stain, as distinct from the special stains.

questions.title: The name of the mitochondrion's inner folds
questions.question: The inner folds of mitochondria are called:-

explanations.A: Correct. The mitochondrion's inner membrane folds inward repeatedly to form cristae. This folding greatly increases the surface area available inside the organelle. That extra surface holds the electron transport chain enzymes that carry out oxidative phosphorylation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The matrix is the space enclosed by the inner membrane, holding the mitochondrion's own DNA and the Krebs cycle enzymes — a compartment, not the folds themselves.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Stroma is not the term for mitochondrial inner-membrane folds; it more commonly refers to the supporting framework of an organ.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Saccules describe flattened membrane-bound compartments such as those of the Golgi apparatus, not the mitochondrion's folds.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cisternae likewise describe flattened membranous spaces, characteristic of the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, not the mitochondrion's inner folds.

questions.learning_objective: Name cristae as the mitochondrion's inner membrane folds.

questions.title: The classification of the goblet cell
questions.question: Goblet cell is example of:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. A multicellular gland is built of more than one secretory cell; the goblet cell is, by definition, the single-cell (unicellular) example instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A serous gland secretes a thin, watery, enzyme-rich fluid; the goblet cell secretes mucus, not a serous product.
explanations.C: Correct. The goblet cell is the standard example of a unicellular exocrine gland. It is a single flask-shaped, mucus-secreting cell scattered within a surface epithelium, respiratory or intestinal. It needs no duct, because it already sits on the very surface it secretes onto.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A muco-serous gland is a multicellular gland with both mucous and serous secretory units (as in the salivary glands), not a description of the single-cell goblet cell.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A waxy (sebaceous-type) gland secretes an oily/waxy product by holocrine secretion; the goblet cell is a mucous, not a waxy, unicellular gland.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the goblet cell as the standard example of a unicellular gland.

questions.title: The connective tissue fibre in the aorta and large vessels
questions.question: What is the type of connective tissue fibers present in aorta and large blood vessels:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Collagen (white fibrous) fibres are present and contribute tensile strength, but they are not the fibre that dominates and defines an elastic artery's wall.
explanations.B: Correct. The aorta and other large, elastic (conducting) arteries have a tunica media built of many concentric, fenestrated elastic laminae. Elastic fibres are what dominate that wall, not collagen and not smooth muscle. Their elasticity lets the wall stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, smoothing the heart's pulsatile output.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Reticular fibres form the fine supporting stroma of parenchymatous organs, not the dominant fibre of a large elastic artery's wall.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Oxytalan fibres are elastic-system fibres found mainly in the periodontal ligament, not the characteristic fibre of the aortic wall.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Purkinje fibres are specialised cardiac conducting myocytes, not a connective tissue fibre at all.

questions.learning_objective: Name elastic fibres as the dominant connective tissue fibre of the aorta and other large arteries.

questions.title: The CT cell activated during wound healing
questions.question: If you had a wound in your hand, which CT cell will be activated at this site during healing:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pigment cells (melanocytes) produce melanin; they are not the cell activated for tissue repair at a wound.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Plasma cells synthesise antibodies as part of adaptive immunity; new collagen synthesis for wound repair is not their role.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mast cells release histamine and heparin in acute inflammation and allergic responses, not the matrix-building activity of healing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adipose cells store fat; they are not activated for tissue repair.
explanations.E: Correct. The fibroblast is the connective tissue cell activated at a wound site. Signalled by the injury's inflammatory and growth-factor cues, it proliferates and migrates into the wound. There it synthesises the new collagen and ground substance that build granulation tissue and, eventually, the scar.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the fibroblast as the connective tissue cell activated during wound healing.

questions.title: The chromosome content of the daughter cell of meiosis
questions.question: In humans, the daughter cell of meiosis contains:-

explanations.A: Correct. The final product of meiosis, the mature gamete, is haploid with 23 chromosomes of a single chromatid each, 23-s. Meiosis I halves the chromosome number to 23, but each of those is still double, 23-d. Meiosis II then separates the sister chromatids to leave the final 23-s complement.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 46-s describes a normal somatic (diploid) cell in G1, before any meiotic reduction — not a product of meiosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 46-d describes the doubled somatic complement after S-phase replication (mitotic G2/prophase), not a meiotic gamete.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 48-d does not correspond to any normal human cell-cycle or meiotic stage.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 92-s does not correspond to any normal human chromosome count at any stage.

questions.learning_objective: State that the final gamete of meiosis is haploid with 23 single-chromatid chromosomes (23-s).

questions.title: The biochemical identity of the membrane's electron-dense layer
questions.question: The electron dense layer of cell membrane is biochemically identified as:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Carbohydrate sits on the membrane's outer face as part of the glycocalyx; it is not the electron-dense structural layer itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glycolipid is a minor membrane component, not the main biochemical identity of its electron-dense structural layer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This names a location within the bilayer rather than a biochemical substance, and does not correctly identify what the electron-dense layer is made of.
explanations.D: Correct. The plasma membrane's trilaminar appearance on electron microscopy comes from its phospholipid bilayer. Each phospholipid's polar phosphate head group is electron-dense and faces one of the two aqueous surfaces. The non-polar fatty acid tails are electron-lucent and face each other in the membrane's middle, producing the light middle band between two dark lines.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cholesterol sits interspersed within the phospholipid bilayer, modulating membrane fluidity, but the electron-dense layer itself is identified by its phospholipid, not by cholesterol.

questions.learning_objective: Identify phospholipid as the biochemical basis of the cell membrane's electron-dense trilaminar appearance.

questions.title: The organelle protecting the cell from drugs and toxins
questions.question: Which organelle protects the cell from damaging effect of medications and toxins:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ribosomes translate protein; detoxification of drugs and toxins is not their function.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Microtubules provide structural tracks and support; they play no role in drug or toxin detoxification.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Secretory vesicles carry material for export; they are not the site of detoxification.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The rough endoplasmic reticulum synthesises secretory and membrane protein; detoxification is instead the smooth ER's job.
explanations.E: Correct. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum is particularly abundant in hepatocytes, the liver's main functional cell. It houses the cytochrome P450 enzyme system, which metabolises and detoxifies drugs, medications and other lipid-soluble toxins. This detoxifying role sits alongside its other jobs of lipid synthesis and calcium regulation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the smooth endoplasmic reticulum as the organelle that detoxifies drugs and toxins.

questions.title: The structure microtubules are found in
questions.question: Microtubules are present in the:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Microvilli are built of a core of actin microfilaments, not microtubules.
explanations.B: Correct. Flagella, and cilia, are built on an axoneme, a 9+2 arrangement of microtubule doublets. Those doublets slide against each other, powered by the motor protein dynein. That sliding is what generates the flagellum's beating motion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cleavage furrow that pinches a dividing cell in two is formed by a contractile ring of actin microfilaments and myosin, not microtubules.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The sarcomere, the contractile unit of striated muscle, is built of actin (thin) and myosin (thick) filaments, not microtubules.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The nuclear envelope is a double membrane structure; it is not built of microtubules, though microtubule-organising activity is involved in its breakdown during mitosis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the flagellum's axoneme as a microtubule-built structure.

questions.title: The connective tissue fibre that is argyrophilic
questions.question: Which of the following fibers is argyrophilic:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. White collagen (type I) fibres are demonstrated by Masson's trichrome or van Gieson, not by their affinity for silver.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Elastic fibres need their own special stains (Verhoeff's, orcein), not silver impregnation.
explanations.C: Correct. Reticular fibres, type III collagen, are argyrophilic. They take up silver stain avidly, appearing black on silver impregnation. This is how their fine, branching network is demonstrated, since they are invisible on routine H&E.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Oxytalan fibres are part of the elastic fibre system and are not the fibre type defined by argyrophilia.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Purkinje fibres are cardiac conducting cells, not a connective tissue fibre, and are not defined by a silver-staining property.

questions.learning_objective: Identify reticular fibres as the argyrophilic (silver-staining) connective tissue fibre.

questions.title: The character of autonomic ganglia
questions.question: The autonomic ganglia are characterized by:-

options.A: Their cell bodies are mostly of the small uniform size
options.D: Have complete capsule of satellite cells

explanations.A: Correct. Autonomic, sympathetic or parasympathetic, ganglia contain multipolar neurons. Their cell bodies are smaller than a dorsal root ganglion's large, uniform sensory neurons. This smaller size is the standard descriptor used to tell an autonomic ganglion apart from a sensory one on a section.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Spinal sensory neurons belong to the dorsal root ganglion, not to an autonomic ganglion, whose neurons are motor (autonomic efferent), not sensory.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Autonomic ganglion neurons are motor (postganglionic autonomic) neurons, not sensory neurons of any kind, sympathetic included.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A complete satellite-cell capsule is the dorsal root (sensory) ganglion's feature; autonomic ganglion neurons have a less complete satellite investment.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Autonomic ganglia are relatively richly vascularised, reflecting their ongoing synaptic activity — poor blood supply instead describes the dorsal root ganglion.

questions.learning_objective: Contrast the autonomic ganglion's smaller, size-uniform multipolar neurons with the dorsal root ganglion's large pseudounipolar ones.

questions.title: The shape of spinous-layer cells
questions.question: The cells of spinous layer are:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Spinous-layer cells are not simply rounded; their many-sided, angular shape is what the term polyhedral captures.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cuboidal cells are roughly cube-shaped with equal dimensions on each side; the spinous layer's cells, pressed against their many neighbours, are polyhedral instead.
explanations.C: Correct. The stratum spinosum's cells are polyhedral, many-sided, in shape. They are joined by desmosome-anchored intercellular bridges. During fixation the tissue shrinks and those bridges appear as spine-like projections, which is what gives the layer its name.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Columnar cells are taller than wide, a shape characteristic of certain glandular or absorptive epithelia, not the epidermis's spinous layer.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Squamous (flat) cells describe the epidermis's most superficial living layers and its dead horny layer, not the deeper, polyhedral spinous layer.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the spinous layer's cells as polyhedral.

questions.title: A character of neuroepithelium
questions.question: Which of the following is a character of neuroepithelium:-

options.C: They are formed of sensory and supporting cells only
options.D: The supporting cells act as precursors for sensory cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neuroepithelium is specialised for sensory reception, not secretion; secretion is a glandular epithelium function.
explanations.B: Correct. Neuroepithelium's sensory cells are modified to receive a sensory stimulus, and the taste cells of the taste bud are the standard example. Their apical surface carries microvilli that extend into the taste pore. This increases the surface area available for receiving the stimulus, the dissolved substance being tasted.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This description is too restrictive — neuroepithelium is defined by having sensory cells modified as receptors, but is not limited to only two named cell categories in every account of it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Supporting cells sustain and structurally support the sensory cells; being their developmental precursor is not the standard character attributed to them.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Covering body surfaces broadly describes surface (covering) epithelium in general, not the specific sensory character that defines neuroepithelium.

questions.learning_objective: State that neuroepithelium's sensory cells carry apical microvilli.

questions.title: How gland cells release their secretions
questions.question: Many gland cell release their secretions through:-

explanations.A: Correct. Exocytosis is the reverse of endocytosis. A cytoplasmic secretory vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and discharges its contents to the outside, without ever breaking the membrane's continuity. This is the standard mechanism by which a merocrine gland releases its product.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Phagocytosis is a form of endocytosis (bringing solid particles into the cell), the opposite direction of movement from secretion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Receptor-mediated endocytosis brings a specific ligand into the cell via a clathrin-coated pit; it is an uptake mechanism, not a secretion one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fluid pinocytosis takes in extracellular fluid; like the other endocytosis options, it moves material into rather than out of the cell.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Endocytosis broadly is the uptake of material into the cell, the reverse process from the secretion the question asks about.

questions.learning_objective: Identify exocytosis as the mechanism by which gland cells release their secretions.

questions.title: A character of intermediate filaments
questions.question: Which of the followings is a character of intermediate filaments:-

options.D: Form the basal body of the cilia

explanations.A: Correct. Each tissue expresses its own characteristic intermediate filament protein: keratin in epithelium, desmin in muscle, vimentin in mesenchyme, glial fibrillary acidic protein in astrocytes, neurofilament in neurons. Immunohistochemical staining for these proteins can therefore reveal a cell's tissue of origin even once it has lost its normal architecture. This makes intermediate filament typing diagnostically important for identifying a poorly differentiated tumour's origin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Myosin forms the thick filament of the actin-myosin contractile system, not an intermediate filament.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Intermediate filaments are structural and supportive, not contractile — contractility belongs to the actin-myosin system instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The basal body, which organises a cilium's axoneme, is built of microtubule triplets (structurally related to the centriole), not intermediate filaments.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Intermediate filaments are about 8-10 nm in diameter, intermediate between the thinner microfilaments (~5-7 nm) and thicker microtubules (~25 nm) — 6-7 nm undersizes them.

questions.learning_objective: Relate tissue-specific intermediate filament proteins to their diagnostic value in identifying a tumour's origin.

questions.title: An endogenous pigment
questions.question: Which of the followings is an endogenous pigment:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Carotene is a dietary, plant-derived pigment absorbed from food, an exogenous source, not one the body itself manufactures.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Inhaled or ingested minerals accumulating in tissue (as in pneumoconiosis) are exogenous material, not a pigment the body produces.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dust is inhaled particulate matter, an exogenous inclusion (as in anthracosis), not an endogenous pigment.
explanations.D: Correct. Melanin is an endogenous pigment. It is synthesised by the body's own melanocytes from the amino acid tyrosine. This is unlike an exogenous pigment such as carotene, dust, minerals or tattoo ink, all of which enter the body from outside rather than being made by it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Tattoo marks are exogenous pigment particles deliberately introduced into the dermis from outside the body.

questions.learning_objective: Classify melanin as an endogenous pigment, as distinct from exogenous pigments and particulate inclusions.

questions.title: The collagen type in the basal lamina
questions.question: What type of collagen is present in basal lamina of basement membrane:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Type I collagen forms the strong, bundled fibres of connective tissue proper, tendon and bone, not the basal lamina.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Type II collagen is the fine fibre of cartilage, not the basal lamina.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Type III collagen is the reticular fibre of organ stroma, not the basal lamina.
explanations.D: Correct. Type IV collagen is not fibrous in form at all, unlike the other collagen types. Instead it forms a granular, sheet-like network within the basal lamina of the basement membrane. It is secreted by the epithelial cells that rest on that basal lamina.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Type V collagen is a minor fibril-associated collagen; the basal lamina's defining collagen is type IV.

questions.learning_objective: Name type IV collagen as the collagen type of the basal lamina.

questions.title: The site rich in hyaluronic acid
questions.question: Which of the following sites have much hyaluronic acid in their matrix:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Large blood vessel walls are dominated by elastic and collagen fibres and smooth muscle, not a hyaluronic-acid-rich mucoid matrix.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mediastinum is not characterised by a hyaluronic-acid-rich mucoid ground substance.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The stroma of parenchymatous organs is supported mainly by reticular fibres, not a mucoid, hyaluronic-acid-rich matrix.
explanations.D: Correct. Wharton's jelly is the mucoid connective tissue of the umbilical cord. It is a soft, jelly-like ground substance rich in hyaluronic acid. The vitreous humour of the eye and the pulp of the teeth are the other classic sites of this same mucoid connective tissue type.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The basal lamina's matrix is dominated by type IV collagen and laminin, not a hyaluronic-acid-rich mucoid ground substance.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Wharton's jelly of the umbilical cord as a site rich in hyaluronic acid.
questions.module_subject: MANS-HBG > Histology > Connective Tissue > Mucoid connective tissue

questions.title: The CT cell secreting eosinophil chemotactic factor
questions.question: Which of the following CT cells secretes eosinophil chemotactic factor:-

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fibroblasts synthesise collagen and ground substance; eosinophil chemotactic factor is not among their products.
explanations.B: Correct. The mast cell's granules store heparin and histamine, but not only those two. They also store eosinophil chemotactic factor of anaphylaxis, ECF-A. Once the cell degranulates, ECF-A recruits eosinophils to the site of the allergic reaction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Plasma cells secrete antibodies, not eosinophil chemotactic factor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adipose cells store and release fat; they do not secrete this chemotactic factor.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Macrophages secrete their own set of cytokines and chemotactic signals, but eosinophil chemotactic factor specifically is a mast cell granule product.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the mast cell as the source of eosinophil chemotactic factor of anaphylaxis.
